newsitem.title: USA: Stocks, bonds fall as oil prices soar, dollar falls.
newsitem.headline: Stocks, bonds fall as oil prices soar, dollar falls.

text.p: Blue-chip stocks and bonds fell on Wednesday as crude oil prices shot up, reviving fears of inflation and rising U.S. interest rates.
The dollar fell against the yen after a report showed surging optimism among big Japanese manufacturers, suggesting Japan's huge trade surplus with the United States will continue to grow.
The Dow Jones industrial average dropped 68.08 points to 7,689.98, giving back a large chunk of Tuesday's 153-point gain.
In the broader market, declining issues led advances 1,558 to 1,254 on volume of 603 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.

Stocks spent the day swinging sharply from the plus to the minus column but the market took a sharp downturn on news that OPEC reached an agreement to limit overproduction, which is meant to boost oil prices and could feed inflation.

Wall Street's concern about the impact of higher oil prices was reflected in the inflation-sensitive bond market, where the 30-year Treasury fell 19/32, or $5.94 on a $1,000 bond, raising its yield to 6.74 percent from 6.69 percent Tuesday. The price and yield move in opposite directions.
Meanwhile, crude oil for August delivery rose 49 cents to $19.52 a barrel on the New York Mercantile Exchange.
The Organisation of Petroleum Exporting Countries, which met in Vienna, said the 11-member oil cartel had agreed to retain its 25.03 million barrels a day ceiling until the end of the year.
More significantly, it said that OPEC members agreed to stick to their export quotas, which implied that the producers would stop pumping the 2 million barrels a day in excess of the quota limit.
"We have a very high level of commitment ... 100 percent," said Saudi Arabian Oil Minister Ali Naimi.
The Libyan president of OPEC, Abdullah Salem al-Badri, said production "should go down" as a result of promises given in Vienna.

Analysts said the financial markets were also unnerved by rumours that a major seller of Treasury bonds might be a foreign central bank. An unidentified seller unloaded $1 billion of 10-year notes, which sent the bond market reeling.

"The market is very nervous. The Dow travelled ... back and forth today with nothing concrete. There were rumours of foreigners selling in bonds and crude rose slightly after OPEC," said said Michael Metz, chief investment strategist at Oppenheimer & Co.

Analysts said comments by Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin Wednesday did not calm the markets, which were rocked Monday after a remark by Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto sparked fears Japan might sell some of its large holdings of Treasury bonds. Rubin said there was no reason to expect such sales and that the market could absorb them if they occurred.
The dollar fell to 113.83 yen late Wednesday from 114.92 on Tuesday. It also fell to 1.7241 German marks from 1.7245.
Corn prices fell to their lowest level in more than two years as crop-growing weather in the U.S. Midwest turned nearly ideal, enhancing crop production prospects.
At the Chicago Board of Trade, corn for July delivery touched a low of $2.55-3/4 a bushel, the lowest level for the nearby contract since May 1995. July closed four cents lower at $2.56-1/4.
At the Chicago Mercantile Exchange, feeder cattle futures closed higher, boosted by the falling cost of key feed ingredients such as corn.

Feeder cattle for August delivery closed 0.300 cent per pound higher at 78.600 cents. The CME's index of feeder cattle prices in the cash market was up 0.59 cent at 77.56 cents per pound, the highest since August 18, 1994.
Overseas, London's FTSE 100 added 43.7 points to 4,640.0. In Tokyo, the 225-share Nikkei average jumped 337.34 points to 20,679.27.
